Bhugtan Payment Systems: Choosing a Moat

Bengaluru, 21 September 2026

On the Monday morning this case opens, Meher Anand, co-founder and chief executive of Bhugtan Payment Systems, sat in the fourth-floor office in HSR Layout with three one-page memos in front of her, each arguing for a different use of the same money. The board would meet on 9 October, eighteen days away, and expected a single recommendation for how Bhugtan would spend the ₹20 crore of discretionary product budget freed up by the Series C round, not a menu for the board to relitigate. Every rupee had a champion inside the company, and each was, in Meher's judgement, arguing from a fair reading of the same facts.

The company

Meher and her co-founder, Ishaan Verma, started Bhugtan in 2019 after four years on the risk engineering team at a large Bengaluru fintech. Bhugtan builds the payment gateway, reconciliation and settlement APIs behind a merchant's checkout page: a D2C skincare brand, a regional quick-commerce app, or a garment exporter can plug in Bhugtan's SDK and accept UPI, cards and net-banking without building that infrastructure themselves. The business sits in the crowded middle of India's payments stack, competing for the same API-first merchants that Razorpay, Cashfree, PayU and Pine Labs pursue, rather than the consumer wallets PhonePe and Paytm own. By the end of FY26, Bhugtan processed roughly ₹20,000 crore of annualised transaction value across 42,000 merchants and earned ₹63.9 crore of net revenue on that volume, funded through a Series A, a Series B and, fourteen months earlier, a ₹180 crore Series C. Sixteen months of runway remained at the current burn rate — the arithmetic reason the board wanted one clear bet, not three small ones.

The situation

Three events in August forced the choice. First, a fraud ring exploited a gap in Bhugtan's rules engine and drained roughly ₹40 lakh from eleven small merchants in one week before the risk team, led remotely from Toronto, caught the pattern. Second, three of Bhugtan's twenty largest D2C merchants told their account managers they were evaluating Cashfree over pricing, and Ishaan's Pune team, who field every migration ticket, argued that only deeper integration into merchants' accounting and inventory software would make switching costly enough to stop this becoming routine. Third, Arjun Malhotra, Bhugtan's enterprise sales head, working from New Jersey to cover both his Gulf and North American conversations, had spent five months courting the finance office of a large Dubai-based sourcing conglomerate that wanted to route roughly ₹2,500 crore a year of exporter payments through a single rail, provided Bhugtan secured cross-border aggregator authorisation from the Reserve Bank of India within two quarters. Each event pointed to a different durable advantage Bhugtan might build, and Meher could not fund all three at the level each champion said it needed.

The people

Meher Anand — Co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru

Meher owns the decision and the board relationship. She wants a bet the board will still respect in two years, not merely one that improves next quarter's revenue line.

Ishaan Verma — Co-founder and CTO, Pune

Ishaan controls the fourteen-engineer team that would build any of the three options. He wants the ERP and accounting-software integrations funded first, because his team already absorbs the cost of churn in support tickets and sees switching costs as the fastest way to stop the bleeding.

Bhavya Kulkarni — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto

Ananya built Bhugtan's original fraud model and argues that a shared risk-signal network, pooling anonymised fraud patterns across all 42,000 merchants, is the only advantage that compounds: the more merchants join, the better the signal, the lower the losses, the more merchants it attracts.

Arjun Malhotra — Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey

Arjun has the Dubai relationship nearly closed and wants the compliance and engineering resource to finish it, arguing that no Indian payments company has yet built a serious position in Gulf-bound exporter payments, and that Bhugtan could own the category before Razorpay or Cashfree notice it.

The exhibits

Before the August events, Meher had asked her finance team to break Bhugtan's revenue down by merchant segment, shown in Exhibit 1. The domestic direct-to-consumer segment, which uses only the bare API, carries the highest churn and the most revenue at risk; the cross-border, ERP-integrated exporters churn least, because migrating means re-plumbing their accounting systems. This is the pattern Ishaan points to.

Exhibit 1 also frames Ananya's argument, even though it does not mention fraud directly: Bhugtan's own fraud losses ran to roughly ₹12 crore in FY26, or 0.06 per cent of total transaction value, concentrated in the domestic D2C segment where signal is thinnest. Durability estimated qualitatively by the case writer from how easily a rival with comparable capital could replicate each mechanism within eighteen months.

The options

Option 1 — Fund the ERP and accounting integrations

For ₹6 crore, Ishaan's team can build native connectors into Tally, Zoho Books and two widely used inventory platforms over the next year, raising the cost of leaving Bhugtan for the 25,000 domestic D2C merchants. Exhibit 2 shows this retains ₹2.69 crore a year once churn falls from 22 to 10 per cent, a 27-month payback — the slowest of the three, but the advantage, once built, does not erode simply because a competitor matches Bhugtan's price.

Option 2 — Build the shared fraud-signal network

For ₹9 crore over eighteen months, Ananya's team can build the pooled-signal risk engine, cutting fraud losses from ₹12 crore to ₹4 crore a year, an 8 crore saving and a 14-month payback. Because the signal improves with every merchant who joins, this is the option closest to a genuine network effect, but it also asks the two India-based engineering pods to split attention across risk infrastructure and everything else on their roadmap for over a year.

Option 3 — Chase the Gulf exporter corridor

For ₹5 crore of compliance, licensing and engineering effort, Arjun's Dubai relationship converts into ₹2,500 crore of new annual transaction value and ₹7.5 crore of new revenue, an 8-month payback, the fastest of the three. It also depends on a single client and on the Reserve Bank granting a cross-border aggregator authorisation inside two quarters, and once the corridor is visible, Razorpay or Cashfree could copy it with their far larger balance sheets.

Questions for discussion

  1. What does each of the three events in August reveal about where Bhugtan is currently exposed, and which of the 7 Powers, if any, does Bhugtan already possess?
  2. Using Exhibit 2, which option delivers the best return on the ₹20 crore in the next eighteen months, and does the fastest payback also build the most durable advantage?
  3. How should Meher weigh a single-client, first-mover position in the Gulf corridor against a slower-compounding network effect at home?
  4. Given the engineering capacity described for Pune and Toronto, can Bhugtan credibly fund two options rather than choosing one, and what would have to be true for that to work?

A note for the learner

The 7 Powers framework asks a narrower question than "which option grows revenue fastest": it asks which option, once built, keeps competitors from taking the resulting profit away. Judged only on payback, Option 3 wins comfortably; judged on durability, it is the weakest, because counter-positioning works only as long as larger, better-capitalised rivals find the segment unattractive to copy, and a confirmed ₹2,500 crore corridor is exactly the kind of proof that removes that protection. Option 1 builds real switching costs, but slowly, and does nothing about the fraud exposure that is already costing Bhugtan ₹12 crore a year. Option 2 is the only one of the three that compounds: every merchant who joins improves the shared signal for every other merchant, which is the definition of a network effect and the closest thing on this list to Ananya's cornered resource in fraud data. A well-reasoned answer does not need to reject Options 1 and 3 outright, but it should recognise that Bhugtan has one true moat candidate among the three and should fund it first, using the faster-paying Gulf relationship, scaled to a size the compliance team can support without the single-client risk Exhibit 2 implies, as a secondary, self-limited bet rather than the primary one. The defensible path: commit ₹9 crore to the fraud-signal network now, cap the Dubai relationship to a pilot near ₹800 crore of annual volume until the RBI authorisation and a second anchor client are both in hand, and revisit the ERP integrations at the next funding round once the network effect has data to show the board.

Strategy & Business · Competitive Strategy & Moats

Moats and the 7 Powers

Which durable source of advantage could we plausibly earn — and how do we know it is real before a well-funded rival tests it for us?

On the second Monday of September 2026, Rohan Iyer, VP of Product at Meenakshi Supply, opened a spreadsheet he had been avoiding for a week. Meenakshi Supply ran a business-to-business platform out of Chennai that let restaurants and cloud kitchens order raw materials — vegetables, dairy, packaging, dry goods — from a vetted network of wholesalers, with the platform handling ordering, short-term working-capital credit, and delivery tracking. In seven years the company had signed 14,200 active restaurant accounts across Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad and, since 2024, Pune, running at a gross-merchandise-value rate of roughly ₹640 crore a year. Meenakshi took a blended 4.5% of that GMV in commission and financing spread, which put annual revenue near ₹28.8 crore, and its net revenue retention — the rate at which existing accounts kept spending more, net of churn — had held above 115% for three straight years. By the standards of Indian B2B commerce, it was a well-run, profitable, unglamorous business.

The spreadsheet was about a much less comfortable business: Manthan Mandi, a nine-month-old competitor that had launched in Chennai with no app, no credit product and no sales team — just a WhatsApp number, a fleet of hired pickup trucks, and prices sourced directly from wholesale mandis that ran 6 to 9% below Meenakshi's on produce. Manthan was not chasing Meenakshi's best customers. It was going after the roughly 30% of Meenakshi's accounts, by headcount, that ran under ₹15,000 a month in orders and rarely touched the credit line — dhabas and small tiffin centres that valued rock-bottom price over anything else. That segment was only 9% of Meenakshi's GMV, but it was growing, and three of Rohan's regional managers had already reported accounts flipping to Manthan entirely. In eighteen days Rohan had to walk into a board meeting and recommend one of three moves: cut prices platform-wide to blunt Manthan everywhere, build a stripped-down, cash-only product to fight Manthan on its own turf, or hold price and defend the business a different way. Getting this wrong in either direction — panicking into a price war the company's own gross margin could not survive, or dismissing a real threat as noise — would show up in the numbers within two quarters. What Rohan needed, before he could recommend anything, was a way to tell the difference between an advantage that merely existed today and one that would still exist after Manthan had studied it closely and tried to take it apart.

What a moat actually is

The word "moat" entered business vocabulary informally — Warren Buffett used it in Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters through the 1980s and 1990s to describe a business protected from competitors the way a castle is protected by water, and the metaphor stuck because it captures something true: some businesses keep earning returns above their cost of capital for decades, while others that look just as good on a product-review site get their margins competed away within a few years. But a metaphor is not a method. "We have a moat" tells a founder nothing about which of several very different mechanisms is actually doing the protecting, how strong it is, or when it will stop working. That gap is what Hamilton Helmer, a strategy consultant and investor who has taught the subject at Stanford's Graduate School of Business, set out to close in his 2016 book 7 Powers. Helmer's claim, backed by case histories across a century of American business, was that durable competitive advantage — what he called a "power" — always reduces to one of exactly seven distinct mechanisms, and that each one only counts as real if it passes a two-part test: it must produce a measurable Benefit, meaning a real difference in cash flow versus a competitor without it, and it must be protected by a Barrier, meaning a structural reason a rival cannot simply copy it even after fully understanding it. The single sentence Rohan could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: a moat is not a feature you built, it is a reason a well-funded, well-informed rival still cannot take your margin even after they have seen exactly what you did.

Figure 1. Helmer's test: a "power" requires both a benefit and a barrier. Differentiation without a barrier erodes; a barrier that protects nothing valuable is irrelevant.

The mechanics, walked through with Meenakshi's own candidates

Applying the test properly means doing four things most practitioners do implicitly, badly, or not at all. First, name the arena precisely — a power is always relative to a specific, bounded competitive contest, not the whole economy; Meenakshi's relevant arena was "B2B raw-material supply to independent restaurants and cloud kitchens in south Indian metros," not "Indian food-tech." Second, identify which of the seven mechanisms is even plausible given the assets the company actually has, rather than reaching for whichever one sounds most impressive in a pitch deck. Third, and this is the step almost everyone skips, prove the barrier — not merely that a rival would have to spend money to copy you, since any well-funded rival can spend money, but that spending money specifically would not work, because of a structural reason: a patent, a contract, a physical scarcity, a network that only exists once it exists, or an asymmetry that punishes the copier and not the original. Fourth, test the claim at the level of price: if the power is real, the firm should be able to sustain a price or margin that a fully informed customer would still accept rather than switch, even knowing a cheaper alternative exists.

Rohan ran three candidates through this sequence. The first was scale economies: as GMV grew, the fixed cost of underwriting restaurant credit risk and building delivery routes got spread over more volume, letting Meenakshi run at lower per-account cost than a smaller entrant. That is a real mechanism — Helmer's scale economies power — but its barrier depends on the fixed cost actually staying fixed while volume grows, and Rohan found that Meenakshi's largest wholesaler partners had already given the platform their maximum volume discount tier at around 8,000 restaurant accounts; the marginal scale benefit above that had flattened two years earlier. The advantage was real but no longer growing, and more importantly it was not the thing under attack — Manthan's price edge came from skipping underwriting and platform overhead entirely, not from being under-scaled.

The second candidate, which two of Rohan's colleagues had been calling a "network effect" in planning meetings, did not survive the test at all. The claim was that more restaurants on the platform attracted more wholesalers, which improved assortment and pricing, which attracted more restaurants — a self-reinforcing loop. But when Rohan checked whether adding restaurant number 14,201 measurably improved the terms available to restaurant number one, the answer was no: wholesaler discounts were already saturated at the volume tier Meenakshi had reached years earlier, so the "network" no longer did any work. It had been a real effect once, during the company's early growth, but it was not what was protecting today's margin — a distinction that mattered because it meant defending against Manthan by talking about network effects would be defending against a threat that was not there.

The third candidate — switching costs, built from the accumulated credit history and menu-and-supplier integration a restaurant built up over time on the platform — was the one worth quantifying carefully, because unlike the first two it appeared to explain exactly why Manthan was winning some accounts and not others.

Figure 2. Only switching costs, and only for one segment of Meenakshi's base, sits in the strong-benefit, strong-barrier quadrant that makes a genuine power.

The arithmetic Rohan actually ran

To turn "switching costs are real" into something a board could act on, Rohan had to price the switching cost in rupees, not adjectives. A restaurant leaving Meenakshi for Manthan gave up an approved working-capital credit line — averaging ₹1.8 lakh across accounts that used it — negotiated at 14% annualised, well below the roughly 18% an NBFC would charge a small restaurant with no track record starting fresh. Rebuilding that trust elsewhere would cost the restaurant the difference, 4 percentage points, on its typical drawn balance: ₹1.8 lakh × 4% ≈ ₹7,200 a year, an annuity Meenakshi's own data showed took new lenders roughly nine months of repayment history to match. Add to that the operational cost of switching — Meenakshi's churn-cohort data showed stockout rates spiking from a baseline of 2% to 14% in the first sixty days after a restaurant moved its ordering to an unfamiliar supplier, plus an average 11 hours of staff time re-keying a supplier catalogue into a new workflow. That bundle — roughly ₹7,200 a year in interest plus a real, if harder to price, risk of running out of onions on a Friday night — is the switching cost, and it only exists for restaurants that actually draw on the credit line.

Set against that is what Manthan actually offers: a 7% saving on a typical ₹38,000 monthly raw-material spend, or about ₹2,660 a month, ₹31,920 a year. For an account that draws meaningfully on Meenakshi's credit line, ₹31,920 in savings does not clear a ₹7,200 switching cost plus real stockout risk — the customer stays, and Meenakshi can, in principle, hold its 4.5% take rate on that account without losing it. For an account that never uses the credit line at all — pays cash, orders small — there is no switching cost to overcome, and the ₹31,920 in annual savings is simply free money for moving to Manthan. That is the whole mechanism in one sentence: Manthan was not competing away Meenakshi's moat, it was searching for, and finding, the exact seam where the moat did not reach.

High-credit-usage kitchens70%91%Yes, >₹1L line~28,600~7,200 + stockout riskYes — cost exceeds saving
Small dhabas / tiffin centres30%9%Rarely, or not at all~31,920near zeroNo — nothing to hold them

The second pass is what makes the arithmetic useful rather than merely reassuring. Rohan's team had heard, through a wholesaler contact, that Manthan was preparing to add a lightweight "pay-in-15-days" credit product of its own, funded through a smaller NBFC willing to underwrite thinner files at higher rates. If that launched, the switching cost would not vanish, but it would shrink: restaurants could rebuild a credit relationship faster and more cheaply than the nine-month assumption Rohan had used, which would push some of the currently protected 91% of GMV into the vulnerable category. Rerunning the model with a rebuild period of three months instead of nine roughly doubled the annuity value a switching restaurant would recover in year one, which was enough, in Rohan's sensitivity table, to flip an estimated 25 additional percentage points of GMV from "protected" to "exposed" — taking the vulnerable share from 9% toward 34%. That single changed input was the clearest argument in the deck for why the board's real decision was not about today's 9%, but about whether to widen the switching-cost moat before Manthan's own credit product arrived, not after.

Eight distinctions worth sitting with

1. Being good at something is not the same as being protected for having it

Meenakshi's delivery reliability, at 98% on-time, was genuinely better than Manthan's informal truck network. That is differentiation, and differentiation is valuable — but valuable is not the same as durable. Differentiation without a barrier is a lead that shrinks every quarter a well-resourced competitor keeps trying; a power is a lead that a competitor cannot close no matter how much it tries or spends. The practical tell is to ask not "are we better," but "if a rival matched our resources and studied us for a year, could they close this specific gap" — if the honest answer is yes, given enough time and money, it is an edge, not a moat.

2. A power needs both halves, and most claims quietly drop one

Meenakshi's "network effect" claim had a real benefit once, in 2019 and 2020, but by 2026 it had lost its barrier — any rival could reach the same wholesaler discount tier Meenakshi had, because the tier itself had stopped moving. The reverse failure is just as common: a real barrier protecting a benefit nobody would pay for, such as a proprietary technology that customers do not actually value enough to switch cost anything for. Testing both halves separately, rather than nodding at the word "moat" as a whole, is what catches this.

3. A power is always relative to a specific arena

Meenakshi's switching-cost power existed in the arena of "restaurants that use working capital credit in south Indian metro B2B supply." It did not exist in the arena of cash-paying dhabas, and it might not exist at all if Meenakshi tried to expand into, say, hotel chains with their own centralised procurement, an entirely different competitive contest with different incumbents and different switching costs. A moat statement without a named arena attached to it is usually a moat statement that has not been tested.

4. Counter-positioning works through collateral damage, not just lower cost

Manthan is cheaper because it skips underwriting and platform overhead — but the reason Meenakshi cannot simply copy Manthan's cash-only model tomorrow is not that it is expensive to build. It is that doing so would cannibalise the ₹28.8 crore of margin Meenakshi already earns from its credit business and signal to its best, most profitable accounts that the credit relationship they value is being deprioritised. That asymmetry — where mimicking the attacker actively damages the incumbent's existing, more profitable model — is what Helmer calls counter-positioning, and it is a genuine power for the attacker precisely because the incumbent's own success is what stops it from responding in kind.

5. Which power is available to you changes as the company ages

Helmer's own case histories show a rough sequence: young companies rarely have scale, network density, an installed base of switching costs, or an established brand, because all four take years and volume to accumulate — so early advantage tends to come from counter-positioning (a business model incumbents cannot mimic without hurting themselves) or a cornered resource (an asset a rival simply cannot get, at any price, right now). Scale economies, network economies, switching costs, brand and process power are what a company built on those early foundations grows into later, if it survives long enough to accumulate them.

6. The real proof is a price test, not a satisfaction score

A high customer-satisfaction score or NPS tells you customers like you. It does not tell you whether they would still pay you a premium if a fully informed alternative sat next to you at a lower price — which is precisely the experiment Manthan ran on Meenakshi's behalf, for free. The only test that actually proves a power is whether the firm can hold its price or margin against an informed, motivated alternative without losing the volume it needs. Everything else is a proxy that can mislead a team into confidence it has not earned.

7. Process power is the one people claim most and prove least

It is tempting for any operations-proud team to say "our processes are just better" and call that a moat. Genuine process power — the kind Toyota built over decades inside its production system — requires know-how that is tacit (hard to write down), cumulative (built from years of small, compounding improvements) and organisationally embedded (it lives in how hundreds of people work together, not in a document a rival could read). Most "our ops are better" claims describe a current lead built on a few good hires and a decent playbook, which a well-funded competitor can hire away or reverse-engineer within a couple of years — that is not process power in Helmer's sense, however real the current advantage feels.

8. A moat does not tell you the market is worth defending, and it does not defend itself

Even a genuine, well-tested power says nothing about whether the underlying market is large enough or growing fast enough to be worth the fight — Meenakshi's protected 91% of GMV is only valuable because south Indian B2B restaurant supply is itself a large and growing market; the same switching-cost logic applied to a shrinking category would be a well-defended retreat. Nor does a power hold itself in place: regulatory change, a new distribution channel, or a technology shift — generative-AI-driven procurement tools are already starting to erode exactly this kind of workflow switching cost in adjacent categories — can dissolve a barrier that looked solid a year earlier. A thoughtful newcomer should always ask what would have to change in the world, not in the company, for this specific barrier to stop working.

How this looks different by product type and by company age

In consumer products, the two powers that recur most are branding — a sustained willingness to pay a premium even with full information, built over years of consistent experience, as with Amul in Indian dairy — and network economies, where value rises with the number of other users, as in a social or messaging product. In B2B software and platforms like Meenakshi, switching costs dominate, because the product gets woven into a workflow, a data history and, often, a financing relationship that is genuinely costly to unwind, and process power shows up wherever complex service delivery — enterprise implementation, account management, credit underwriting — accumulates hard-to-copy organisational know-how. In marketplaces, the central and most fragile power is network economies through liquidity: more buyers attract more sellers and vice versa, but marketplaces are also the business type most exposed to multi-homing, where both sides simply join a competing marketplace too, which is exactly why Meenakshi's claimed network effect turned out, on inspection, to have already saturated. Company age changes which powers are even candidates: a two-year-old startup has no scale, no accumulated switching costs and no brand history to draw on, so its only realistic options are counter-positioning against an incumbent's own business model or control of a genuinely scarce resource; a mature company like Meenakshi has the opposite problem, holding several powers that may look intact on a slide but have quietly saturated or eroded, as its network claim had, without anyone noticing until a competitor tested the seam.

Where practitioners go wrong

The first common mistake is declaring a network effect from the observation that usage and user count both went up together, without checking whether a new entrant offering better short-term incentives could rebuild an equivalent network quickly. The symptom is a strategy deck with an arrow-covered "flywheel" diagram and no number attached to it; the underlying error is mistaking correlation between growth and users for proof of a barrier; the cheapest diagnostic is asking whether a rival with, say, eighteen months of subsidised acquisition spend could plausibly reconstruct the same density — if a believable answer is yes, it is not a durable network effect. The second mistake is treating brand marketing spend as automatically moat-building; the symptom is leadership pointing to awareness or recall scores as evidence of pricing power, when the underlying error confuses being known with being trusted enough to command a premium at full information; the diagnostic is a simple parity test — does a customer who is shown both options, with prices and quality made explicit, still choose and pay more for you. The third mistake, the one Rohan was staring at directly, is responding to a counter-positioned entrant by matching its price or its model outright; the symptom is a board proposal to cut prices platform-wide; the underlying error is assuming an incumbent's scale automatically wins a price fight, when the entrant's advantage may come from a structurally lower cost base the incumbent cannot reach without breaking its own more profitable business; the diagnostic is comparing unit economics line by line, not just headline prices, before matching anything. The fourth mistake is mistaking low churn for switching costs when it is really just inertia inside a contract term; the symptom is confidence that customers are "sticky" based on an aggregate churn number; the underlying error is not separating retention that comes from a real economic cost to leave from retention that comes from customers simply not having gotten around to leaving yet; the cheapest diagnostic is watching what churn does specifically at contract renewal or credit-line review dates, when the friction of staying briefly disappears.

A portrait of the decision made well

Three years before Rohan's board meeting, a much smaller company called Mrinal Roasters, a specialty-coffee business founded by two former exporters in Coorg, faced a version of the same question with far less data to work with. Mrinal had signed exclusive, multi-year sourcing contracts with three high-altitude estates producing a distinctive, low-volume varietal that larger roasters had never bothered to lock up, because the volumes were too small to matter to them — a cornered resource, in Helmer's terms, precisely because it was valuable to Mrinal's positioning and irrelevant to everyone bigger. When a well-funded competitor launched a marketing campaign built around nearly identical packaging and language eighteen months later, Mrinal's founders did not panic into a price cut or a redesign. They ran the only test that mattered: did their existing customers still pay the same premium once a cheaper, similarly marketed alternative sat on the same shelf. The answer was yes, because the competitor could describe Mrinal's coffee in its marketing but literally could not buy the same beans — the three estates were under contract, and a rival could not "out-market" a supply constraint. Mrinal's founders spent the resulting eighteen months not defending the brand story, which had already proven it could withstand imitation, but extending their exclusive contracts to two additional estates before any other roaster noticed the model — widening the barrier while it was still working, rather than waiting until a competitor found the seam in it, exactly as Rohan would eventually decide to do with Meenakshi's credit product.

What Rohan decided

Rohan walked into the board meeting and recommended against both extremes. He did not propose cutting Meenakshi's take rate platform-wide, because the arithmetic showed that would give up roughly ₹4.5 crore a year in revenue across the whole 91% of GMV that was already protected, to chase a 9% segment that Manthan could serve more cheaply on structural grounds Meenakshi could not match without cannibalising its own credit business. He did not propose ignoring Manthan either, because the sensitivity analysis on the credit-rebuild period showed the protected 91% could shrink toward two-thirds of GMV within a year if Manthan's own credit product landed before Meenakshi acted. Instead he proposed widening the switching-cost moat downward: a smaller, faster-approved credit product — advances as low as ₹15,000, underwritten on order history alone rather than a full financial file — aimed specifically at the small-dhaba segment that had never had access to Meenakshi's existing line, making the moat reach a segment it had never covered rather than trying to out-discount an opponent whose entire model depended on Meenakshi not doing exactly that. He recommended conceding the smallest, most price-sensitive cash accounts that would never draw meaningful credit regardless, rather than spending capital defending customers who were never going to be profitable to keep. What made the recommendation defensible was not intuition about which accounts felt important, but the price test applied segment by segment: where the switching cost genuinely exceeded what Manthan offered, Meenakshi could hold price; where it did not, the honest move was to let those accounts go rather than destroy value defending them. From here, the topic to study next is pricing power as the test of a moat, because it is the discipline that turns "we believe we have an advantage" into a number a board can act on — and moat erosion and defence, because the switching-cost barrier Rohan was about to widen is precisely the kind that a well-capitalised rival's own credit product, or a shift in how AI tools handle procurement workflows, could narrow again within a few years of being built.

Two questions worth sitting with:

  • If a well-capitalised rival matched every visible feature of your product tomorrow, what would still make your customers pay you a premium — and could you say, in one sentence, exactly why they could not copy that specific thing?
  • Which of your current advantages would survive your own attempt to copy your competitor's business model — and which ones only look durable because no one with the resources to test them has bothered yet?

Pune, the night of Sunday 11 October 2026

1. The night before

The rain over Baner had stopped by nine, and Meghna Chitale had the flat to herself. On the dining table lay four memos, each from a different city, each asking for most of the same money. By nine the next morning she owed the board a single recommendation for the ₹22 crore of growth capital it had approved in August. The board met in Mumbai on Thursday 22 October, and the chairman had been blunt: one bet with a name, not four experiments.

What made the evening difficult was not the money. It was a sentence Sudeep Rane had put at the bottom of his memo from Bengaluru: “All four options assume the console is the product. If that is wrong, all four are wrong.” Lalima's business — 9,400 tinting consoles on 9,400 dealer counters, and the cartridges that fed them — rested on that assumption. Meghna had spent six years defending it.

She had joined in 2020 as the company's first product manager and become chief product officer in 2024. She knew the arithmetic in the memos better than the people who wrote it. What she did not know was which of Lalima's advantages would still be one in 2031.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Lalima Colour Systems was founded in Pune in 2012 by Harish Kamat, who had spent eleven years building dispensing equipment for a paint manufacturer. A homeowner in Kolhapur did not order a colour from a brochure; she stood at a dealer's counter, pointed at a fan deck, and waited while the dealer tinted a base can on the spot. Whoever controlled that counter controlled the sale. The national majors — Asian Paints above all, then Berger, Kansai Nerolac and Indigo Paints — had put their own machines into their own dealers' shops for decades.

Harish's proposition was for everyone else: a brand-neutral console, sold to the dealer rather than given by a manufacturer, able to tint any participating manufacturer's base to any of 14,800 shades in Lalima's own formulation library. The dealer became less dependent on one brand; the regional manufacturer bought shelf presence it could not otherwise get.

Then came the decision that shaped everything after it. In 2018, chasing volume that would take the Pune line to cost parity with imported dispensers, Harish approved a capex bundle: the console outright at ₹1.65 lakh with a perpetual, no-fee licence to the library. Ninety-two per cent of a two-year sales push went out on those terms. It worked — five thousand installations by 2021, unit cost down by a third. It also left 6,200 consoles, 66.0 per cent of today's base, that generate no recurring revenue and cannot be updated remotely, connectivity having been an accessory nobody bought. Of those, the 1,450 built between 2014 and 2017 cannot take a retrofit kit at all. Since 2022 the console has sold at ₹1.95 lakh with library, calibration and firmware on subscription at ₹45,000 a year.

3. The industry

India's decorative paint market is one of the country's most profitable consumer franchises, and in 2026 that stopped being a settled fact. The Aditya Birla group's entry under the Birla Opus brand had spent heavily to place tinting machines in dealerships, and the incumbents had answered with dealer incentives rather than price cuts. Every manufacturer now wanted a firmer claim on the counter, which made a brand-neutral console either more valuable or more threatening.

Three outside facts bore on the memos. The Open Network for Digital Commerce was extending into building materials, which meant a painter in Nashik could soon order against a catalogue that had to describe a shade in machine-readable form — and there was no Indian standard for that. Lalima's library was the nearest thing to one. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act made the fourth option awkward: it asked a shopkeeper to photograph a customer's wall. And the trade's reliance on informal credit made a shopkeeper's willingness to pay ₹499 a month an open question, not a parameter.

Lalima's exposure ran outward too. Engineering sat in Bengaluru, twelve of nineteen people; design in Berlin, data science in Toronto, customer success in Singapore, international sales in New Jersey. Moats and the 7 Powers

A moat is not a property you own. It is a price you can hold, against an informed rival, for a stateable number of years — and the discipline is decomposing that price into the mechanisms that defend each rupee of it.

The competent version of this topic ends with a verdict: we have switching costs, or we have a network effect, or we have nothing. The expert version does not produce a verdict at all. It produces a schedule — this many rupees of our current price gap are defended by this mechanism, for roughly this long, against a rival who would have to spend this much to neutralise it — and then it allocates capital against that schedule. The difference between the two versions is the difference between a strategy offsite and a board decision. What follows is an attempt to teach the second version, using two companies whose moat questions arrive in the same fortnight of October 2026 and look nothing alike.

1. Two decisions, two arenas

On the morning of 9 October 2026, Meera Subramanian, Chief Product Officer of Bhavika Instruments, was in a windowless quality lab on the Sanand road outside Ahmedabad, watching a technician run the same blood sample through two machines. Bhavika made point-of-care haematology and biochemistry analysers — desktop units, roughly the size of a bread bin — sold to standalone pathology labs, nursing homes and small hospital chains. The company had 4,820 analysers in the field, an installed base built patiently since 2013. It sold the hardware at a gross margin of 11%: ₹2.4 lakh a unit, ₹31 crore of revenue in FY26, essentially a cost-recovery exercise. It made its money on the sealed reagent cartridges the analysers consumed, at ₹78 a test and a 62% gross margin, which on an average consumption of about 5,400 tests per analyser per year produced roughly 26.0 million tests and ₹203 crore of revenue. Total FY26 revenue ₹234 crore; gross profit ₹135 crore; EBITDA ₹47 crore. It was, on any spreadsheet, a razor-and-blade business with a moat.

The second machine on the bench was also a Bhavika analyser. What differed was the cartridge. A reagent house in Baddi had reverse-engineered the cartridge for the BH-3, Bhavika's older platform, and was selling a compatible consumable at ₹44 a test through two regional distributors. The BH-3 accounted for 1,832 of the 4,820 installed analysers — 38% of the base, 9.9 million tests a year, ₹77 crore of revenue and ₹48 crore of gross profit. Meera's board met on 22 October. Three options were on the paper in front of her. Lock the platform: add a cryptographic authentication chip to the cartridge and push a firmware update that refuses unauthenticated consumables. Open the platform: publish a certification standard, license third-party cartridge makers, and take a fee. Or cut price and defend on service. Her sales head wanted the chip. Her general counsel had written one sentence in the margin of the paper — "aftermarket tying; CCI" — and underlined it twice.

Eleven days later and 600 kilometres south-east, Kavita Deshpande, co-founder and chief executive of Bhupendra Freight Exchange, was in a Pune office with a corridor map on the wall. Bhupendra matched full-truckload shippers to fleet owners: 61,000 verified trucks, 3,400 shipper accounts, ₹2,940 crore of gross booking value in the twelve months to September 2026, a 3.1% blended take rate and ₹91 crore of net revenue. It had a board meeting on 6 November and ₹78 crore of unallocated growth capital. The fight on the table was between two proposals. The first was to spend it on a fuel-card and FASTag-linked working-capital product for fleet owners, built with an NBFC partner — a product the CFO argued would "make the platform sticky". The second was to spend it concentrating supply on six corridors instead of spreading across fourteen cities. Kavita's own data told her something neither proposal acknowledged: 71% of her verified fleet owners also listed on at least one competing exchange, and her aggregate liquidity numbers, which the board liked, concealed the fact that on several lanes her matching engine was slower than a commission agent with a phone.

Both women were about to make a moat decision. Neither would be helped by being told which of seven powers she had.

2. The idea, and the four camps that will not agree about it

Start with the definition, stated tightly. A power is a condition that lets a firm sustain returns above its cost of capital in a specific competitive arena, and it exists only when two things hold simultaneously: a benefit, a measurable improvement in cash flow relative to a rival without it, and a barrier, a structural reason that rival cannot obtain the same benefit even with full knowledge of how you did it and a reasonable willingness to spend. Both halves are necessary; the framing is Hamilton Helmer's, set out in 7 Powers (2016), which enumerates scale economies, network economies, counter-positioning, switching costs, branding, cornered resource and process power. The word "moat" itself is older and looser — Warren Buffett used it in Berkshire Hathaway letters through the 1980s to describe protected businesses, and it was a metaphor, not a method.

The intellectual history matters because the disagreements are old and still live. Joe Bain's work on barriers to entry in the 1950s put structure at the centre: firms earn rents because industries permit them. Michael Porter's Competitive Strategy (1980) turned that into the five forces, an industry-level lens in which firm-level advantage is largely a positional choice within a given structure. Richard Rumelt's variance-decomposition work in 1991 then embarrassed the structuralists somewhat, finding that business-unit effects explained several times more profit variance than industry effects — which is to say, who you are matters more than where you are. That opened the door for the resource-based view: Birger Wernerfelt in 1984, Jay Barney in 1991 with the VRIN test (valuable, rare, inimitable, non-substitutable), and David Teece and colleagues in 1997 with dynamic capabilities, the argument that what persists is not a resource but the capacity to reconfigure resources. Bruce Greenwald and Judd Kahn's Competition Demystified (2005) pushed back hard from the structuralist side, arguing that there are really only three barriers — supply-side cost advantage, demand-side customer captivity, and economies of scale — and that scale alone is worthless without captivity, because an unattached customer base lets any entrant buy scale. Running underneath all of it is the empirical persistence-of-profits literature, which has consistently found that abnormal returns decay, with estimated half-lives commonly in the five-to-ten-year range for most industries and long tails for a minority of firms.

Four camps, then, and it is worth stating what each would and would not sign, because practitioners routinely borrow a sentence from one camp and a conclusion from another.

Table 1. The four positions, and the proposition each will not concede
CampWill signWill not signIts strongest evidence
Structural / IO (Bain, Porter, Greenwald)"In a fragmented arena with no customer captivity, no amount of operational excellence produces durable rents.""A great team can manufacture a moat in a structurally bad industry."Persistent cross-industry ROIC gaps; the regularity with which excellent firms in commodity arenas earn their cost of capital and no more.
Resource-based / capability (Wernerfelt, Barney, Teece)"Causally ambiguous, path-dependent, organisationally embedded resources explain persistent profit differences between direct rivals in the same arena.""Advantage reduces to entry barriers."Rumelt's variance decomposition; the durability of firms whose advantage nobody can quite specify.
Schumpeterian / transient advantage (Schumpeter, D'Aveni, McGrath)"All rents are temporary. Helmer / practitioner synthesis"Benefit plus barrier is the complete test, and there are exactly seven mechanisms.""Powers can be acquired whenever management decides to; they are available only at moments of industry flux."A century of case histories in which claimed advantages without a barrier reliably evaporated.

The problem this whole apparatus was invented to solve is worth naming plainly, because it is the problem Meera and Kavita actually have. Firms make irreversible, multi-year investments — a cartridge line, a corridor subsidy — whose return depends entirely on whether a price can be held after rivals respond. Accounting gives you last year's margin. Market research gives you customers' stated preferences. Neither tells you the one thing you need: how much of today's margin will still be there after a competent, funded rival has studied you. The moat literature is, at bottom, an attempt to make that forecast falsifiable.

3. Mechanics: decomposing a premium into defended rupees

Experts do six things, of which the middle three are almost always left implicit. First, define the arena as a cell, not an industry: a customer segment crossed with a use occasion crossed with the specific substitutes available to that buyer. Bhavika's arena is not "Indian in-vitro diagnostics" (₹12,000 crore and rising) but "sealed-cartridge consumables for installed BH-series analysers in NABL-accredited labs running 10 to 30 tests a day". Second, observe the realised premium, not the list price: the actual per-unit gap you sustain against the best informed alternative, multiplied by the volume that genuinely stays at that gap. Third — the step that separates this from a slide — decompose that gap into mechanisms by computing, for each, the buyer's indifference point. Fourth, attach a half-life to each rupee: how long before a determined rival neutralises that specific mechanism, and what it would cost them. Fifth, convert to value. Sixth, write down in advance what would falsify the whole schedule.

Take Bhavika's ₹34 gap (₹78 versus the ₹44 compatible cartridge) and work it.

Switching costs. A lab moving to the third-party cartridge must re-validate the method to keep its NABL accreditation intact: twenty paired patient samples, a precision study, documentation, and one external quality assessment cycle. Bhavika's own field data put the cost at about ₹60,000 of technician time and consumables, one-time. Naively, a lab running 5,400 tests a year saves ₹34 × 5,400 = ₹1.84 lakh annually, so it recovers ₹60,000 in under four months; on that arithmetic the switching cost defends nothing. But the right calculation runs the other way: given the switching cost, what is the largest premium the lab would tolerate indefinitely? Amortise ₹60,000 over a three-year horizon at a 14% discount rate (annuity factor 2.32): the defensible premium is ₹60,000 ÷ (5,400 × 2.32) = ₹4.79 per test. Call it ₹5. Practitioners who stop at payback wildly overstate what switching costs buy them; practitioners who stop at the NPV understate it slightly, because real buyers exhibit an inertia wedge — Bhavika's churn cohorts showed labs tolerating roughly ₹7 before moving. The honest figure is ₹5 defended, with ₹2 of behavioural cushion that will disappear the moment a distributor offers to fund the revalidation.

Process power. Bhavika's cartridges showed a coefficient of variation of 1.8% across production lots; the reverse-engineered cartridge tested at 4.6%. That difference is not aesthetic. It drives a repeat-test rate of 2.1% versus 6.8%, and at 5,400 tests that is 254 extra repeats a year, each costing the lab a cartridge plus about ₹95 of technician and reporting time — ₹35,300 a year, or ₹6.5 per test. It also drives EQAS outlier probability, which Bhavika estimated at 3% a year versus 11%; an outlier that becomes an accreditation non-conformance costs a lab roughly ₹2.8 lakh in remediation and six weeks of assessor correspondence, so the expected-cost difference is 8% × ₹2.8 lakh = ₹22,400 a year, another ₹4.1 per test. Total: ₹10.6, call it ₹11. Whether this is genuinely process power rather than a temporary manufacturing lead is a separate question, addressed below; on the evidence of a rival that has been trying for three years and is still at 4.6%, it is at least a barrier with some height.

Cornered resource. Bhavika's membrane came from a single Japanese specialty supplier under an exclusivity that runs to March 2029. The two qualified alternatives cost 2.3 times as much and delivered 6.1% CV. Price that at the cost the rival must bear to match: roughly ₹9 per test of unavoidable cost disadvantage for anyone without the contract.

Residual. ₹34 − 5 − 11 − 9 = ₹9 per test that nothing defends. It is habit, distributor relationships, and the fact that most labs have not yet been called on by someone with a sample of the compatible cartridge. Across 26.0 million tests that is ₹23.4 crore of gross profit a year — very nearly half of FY26 EBITDA — sitting on no barrier at all.

Figure 1. The decomposition is the whole method. A firm that cannot draw this chart for its own product does not know what its moat is worth; a firm that can knows immediately that its defended ceiling is ₹69, that it is currently pricing ₹9 above it, and that the question is not whether to defend but which rupees to concede first.

The fourth step, half-lives, changes the conclusion again. The ₹5 of switching costs is stable but shrinks if a distributor funds revalidation — a cheap move, plausibly within a year. The ₹11 of process power has survived three years of attack and is the longest-lived component, but it decays continuously as the rival's yields improve; Bhavika's own engineering history suggested a competitor moving from 4.6% to 3.0% CV within four years, which would halve that rupee count. The ₹9 of cornered resource does not decay at all — and then falls off a cliff in March 2029. The ₹9 residual has no half-life because it was never alive; it is a stock of customer inattention being consumed at whatever rate the rival's sales force can call on labs.

Finally, convert to value. Helmer's own formalisation is useful here: value equals market scale × growth factor × long-term share × differential margin, or M₀ · g · s̄ · m̄. Bhavika's arena — BH-series-compatible consumables — is about ₹460 crore of annual spend at current prices, growing perhaps 11% a year as small-format labs proliferate; Bhavika holds 96% of it today and might hold 74% at equilibrium once compatibles mature; and the defensible differential margin is the ₹25 of defended premium on a ₹78 price, not the ₹34 it currently charges. Substituting, the durable franchise is worth roughly a third less than the current P&L implies. That number, not the phrase "we have a strong moat", is what belongs in a board paper.

4. The conditions, stated as testable claims

Five conditions govern whether this apparatus tells you the truth. Each is falsifiable, and each behaves differently for the two protagonists.

C1. The premium must be observed at informed indifference. The relevant comparison is what a buyer who knows both options and has quoted both still pays. For Bhavika this holds: the compatible cartridge is physically on the bench, and 62 labs have already switched, giving a real behavioural read. For Bhupendra it fails badly. Two of her four competitors were venture-funded and pricing below cost to buy corridor share; a shipper choosing a rival at a 1.4% take rate is not revealing anything about Bhupendra's barrier, only about someone else's balance sheet. Moat analysis run against a subsidised price is noise, and the correct treatment is to model the rival at its own sustainable cost base, not its current price.

C2. The barrier must punish the copier asymmetrically. Not "expensive to copy" — any funded rival can spend — but "copying costs them more than it costs you, or costs them something they cannot buy". Bhavika's membrane exclusivity qualifies: the rival's disadvantage is a supply constraint, not a spending decision. Bhupendra's proposed fuel-card credit product fails this test as designed, because the NBFC partner underwriting it will happily sign an identical agreement with a rival exchange next quarter; the barrier belongs to the NBFC, not to Bhupendra.

C3. The benefit must be per-unit and must scale with volume you actually hold. Bhavika's ₹25 defended premium applies to every one of 26 million tests. Bhupendra's network benefit, by contrast, is not general at all — it exists only on lanes above a density threshold, which is the substance of section 5.

C4. The substitute set must be stable over the payback horizon. If the relevant alternative in three years is a different technology rather than a cheaper version of yours, the whole decomposition is answering the wrong question. Bhavika's exposure here is real but slow: dry-chemistry and microfluidic architectures could eventually change what a cartridge even is.

C5. The power must survive a change in who does the buying. The most common silent killer of a switching-cost moat is buyer consolidation. Bhavika's single-lab customers bear their own revalidation cost and behave as the model predicts. Its chain customers — a 210-centre diagnostics network is now 14% of cartridge volume — have a central procurement function with an explicit dual-sourcing mandate, and that function does not bear the revalidation cost; a lab manager somewhere does. Against that buyer the ₹5 of switching cost is worth approximately zero.

There are also arenas in which moat thinking is actively misleading. Where prices are administratively capped — as some medical devices have been under India's pricing regulator — a real barrier can be legislated into producing no benefit at all, and the moat analysis will show a fortress earning nothing. Where the arena is being subsidised into existence by capital, current price gaps are meaningless. And where the buyer is procuring under a tender with lowest-compliant-bid rules, the entire mechanism by which a moat converts into margin is switched off by procedure, however real the underlying differentiation.

5. Hard edges: multi-product, two-sided, regulated, hardware-plus-software, AI-native

Multi-product. Bhavika's most instructive error was believing it had one moat. It had two, and they were diverging. On the BH-5 platform the cartridge geometry was patented until 2031 and the membrane exclusivity applied; on the BH-3 the patents had lapsed, the geometry was published in the original regulatory dossier, and the compatible already existed. A single company-level moat statement averaged a strong platform and a collapsing one into a comfortable middle. The expert habit is to compute the schedule per platform, per segment, per geography — Bhavika's BH-3 base in Tier-2 Maharashtra, where the compatible's distributor was strongest, was losing 1.9% of volume a month while the BH-5 base in the south was losing nothing.

Two-sided. Bhupendra's case is the canonical trap. Aggregate liquidity — 61,000 trucks — describes a number that no shipper ever experiences. What a shipper experiences is a lane. Kavita's analysts fitted the relationship on 48 corridors and found that each doubling of trucks available per week on a lane cut median match time by about a third and cut the empty-return rate by roughly seven percentage points, with a visible break: below about 180 trucks per week, the platform's median match time exceeded what an experienced commission agent achieved by phone, and the platform lost the lane not gradually but abruptly, because shippers stopped opening the app at all.

Figure 3. Six of Bhupendra's forty-eight corridors. The company's aggregate liquidity figure is the average of a franchise and a rout. Capital spent below the threshold buys usage; capital spent just above it buys a barrier.

Two further two-sided complications are usually missed. Multi-homing is not symmetric across sides: 71% of Bhupendra's fleet owners multi-home because listing is free and takes ninety seconds, while only 22% of shippers do, because integrating a second exchange into their dispatch system costs real effort. That asymmetry tells Kavita where her switching costs can plausibly be built — on the shipper side — and where they cannot. And cross-side effects can turn negative: beyond a point, adding more trucks to a lane does not help shippers at all and actively hurts fleet owners by cutting their win rate, which is why Bhupendra's fleet-owner churn was highest on its densest corridor.

Regulated. Regulation changes the shape of barriers in three distinct ways that get conflated. It can create one (a licence, an accreditation requirement that raises switching costs, a spectrum allocation); it can destroy one (mandated interoperability, price caps, compulsory unbundling); and it can turn a barrier into a liability, which is Meera's situation. The authentication chip would convert a technical advantage into an aftermarket tie between a durable good and its consumable — precisely the structure that competition authorities in several jurisdictions, India's included, have examined in contexts such as automobile spare parts. The strategic point is not that the chip is illegal; it is that a barrier which depends on a regulator's forbearance has a half-life set by someone else's agenda, and should be valued accordingly.

Hardware plus software. The razor-and-blade structure concentrates the moat question into one number: the ratio of consumable lifetime value to hardware subsidy. Bhavika subsidises ₹2.4 lakh of hardware at 11% margin to capture, over a seven-year analyser life, 37,800 tests at ₹25 of defended margin — about ₹9.45 lakh. That ratio is healthy, but it is also the exact quantity an entrant attacks. A competitor selling an open-architecture analyser at ₹1.45 lakh that accepts any cartridge is not competing on hardware; it is selling the destruction of Bhavika's blade margin as a product feature, and every analyser it places is a permanent subtraction from Bhavika's defended base. The hardware decision and the moat decision are the same decision, which is why they should never sit in different product teams — and in most hardware companies, they do.

AI-native. The pattern worth internalising is that machine-learning capability is the fastest-commoditising layer anyone has yet built a business on, and the barriers migrate outward from it — to proprietary data rights, to workflow switching costs, to distribution, to regulatory permission. The data-flywheel claim in particular deserves arithmetic rather than assertion. If accuracy improves logarithmically with labelled examples — a rough regularity in many applied settings, where each doubling of data buys a fixed increment of error reduction — then a rival needs only a fraction of your corpus to get most of the way. Suppose each doubling cuts error by 12% relative; a rival with one-eighth of your data (three doublings behind) has error about 1.44 times yours. Whether that gap is a moat depends entirely on whether the buyer's indifference price is sensitive to that difference — which returns you, exactly, to the decomposition. A 44% higher error rate on medical triage is decisive; on a marketing subject-line generator it is invisible.

What happens at the organisational seams. Moats die in the gaps between functions. The defended premium sits on the price line, which product does not own; the barrier sits in manufacturing yield or supply contracts, which strategy does not track; the erosion shows up first in discount authorisation, which sales owns and reports as "competitive intensity". Bhavika's median realised discount had drifted from 6% to 14% over two years while list price never moved — the undefended ₹9 was being given away first, quietly, by people whose incentive was volume. Mature companies rarely run anything called a moat audit. What they run, if they are good, is a quarterly price-realisation review by segment, a win/loss analysis specifically on price, a churn-cohort read at the moments when friction disappears (contract renewal, accreditation cycle, a procurement head changing), and a renewal calendar for every exclusive contract. The moat conversation happens inside those four artefacts under other names, which is why asking a mature company "what is your moat" produces a worse answer than asking "show me price realisation by segment for the last eight quarters".

6. Ten nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. A moat is a price, and its unit is the marginal customer's indifference point

The competent practitioner names a power; the expert names a rupee figure and the volume it applies to. The tell in the wild is a strategy document that can describe the moat in a sentence but cannot answer "at what price gap do we start losing volume, and which customers go first?" The obvious reading — that identifying the mechanism is the analytical work — is wrong because mechanisms are cheap to assert and the entire decision content lives in the magnitude. Two companies can both truthfully claim switching costs and have defended premiums of ₹5 and ₹50.

2. The seven powers are not additive, and some are parasitic on others

Decks that list four powers as though they stack are almost always wrong, because scale economies without customer captivity produce no rents at all — an entrant simply buys the customers and thereby buys the scale. The tell is a claim to scale advantage in an arena where customers switch freely and annually. The obvious reading is that more powers means a wider moat; the correct reading is that powers form a dependency graph, and the practitioner's job is to find the one load-bearing mechanism and ask what it rests on.

3. Shape beats height: the half-life matters more than the size of the barrier

A ₹9 barrier that is flat for three years and then vanishes at a contract expiry is more dangerous than a ₹11 barrier eroding 8% a year, because the first produces no signal in any operating metric until the year it fails. The tell is an organisation that debates whether it has a moat but has never dated one. The obvious reading — that a strong barrier is a safe barrier — misses that cliff-shaped risks are precisely the ones management systems are blind to, since every dashboard is built to detect trends.

4. Erosion is consumed from the bottom of the price stack, not the top

When competition arrives, the first thing to go is not list price but realised price, and the rupees given away are exactly the undefended ones, because those are the accounts where the salesperson has no argument to make. The tell is flat list price, flat reported ASP, and quietly deteriorating gross margin by segment. The obvious reading is that margin compression signals cost problems; more often it is the moat schedule revealing itself one discount approval at a time, eighteen months before anyone names it.

5. The person who bears the switching cost is rarely the person who negotiates the price

Switching-cost moats are computed against a fictional unitary buyer. Real organisations split the cost-bearer (the lab technician who must revalidate) from the decision-maker (a central procurement head with a dual-sourcing mandate and a savings target). The tell is churn that spikes within two quarters of a procurement leadership change, or that concentrates entirely in chain accounts while single-site accounts are stable. The obvious reading — that large customers are stickier because integration is deeper — inverts the truth: large customers are often the least protected, because they can afford to internalise the switching cost and are structurally motivated to.

6. Network effects are local and thresholded; global counts are anaesthetic

Almost every real network effect operates within a geography, a lane, a language, a category or a social graph cluster, and exhibits a threshold below which it does not function at all. The tell is a company whose primary liquidity metric has no denominator — total users, total trucks, total listings. The obvious reading is that aggregate scale proves the effect; the correct reading is that aggregate scale can rise while the fraction of arenas above threshold falls, which is the precise signature of a marketplace about to discover it is several weak businesses rather than one strong one.

7. Counter-positioning is a forecast about the incumbent's board, not its engineers

The barrier in counter-positioning is that mimicking the entrant damages the incumbent's existing, more profitable business — so the barrier's strength is a function of how large and how beloved that business remains. The tell that it is expiring is the incumbent creating a separately-governed unit with its own P&L, its own compensation and permission to cannibalise. The obvious reading is that incumbents fail to respond because they are slow or stupid; the accurate reading is that they respond rationally to their own economics, which means the barrier dissolves the moment those economics change — often abruptly, when the legacy business falls below the threshold at which the board will defend it.

8. Cornered resources are usually contracts, and contracts have dates

Exclusive supply, exclusive content, exclusive distribution, a key hire on a retention agreement: nearly every practical cornered resource is a legal instrument with an expiry. The tell is an exclusivity that features prominently in the investor deck and appears nowhere in the operating calendar. The obvious reading is that a cornered resource is the most solid of the powers because it is contractual and verifiable; the correct reading is that this makes it the most precisely perishable, and that renegotiation leverage moves to the counterparty at exactly the moment your dependence on them has been demonstrated by four years of results.

9. Process power is falsified by a hiring test

The honest test of whether operational excellence is a power rather than a good team is counterfactual and uncomfortable: if a well-funded rival hired twelve of your people, could it reproduce the capability within eighteen months? If yes, you have a team, which is valuable and mobile. Genuine process power is tacit, cumulative and distributed across hundreds of people and thousands of small standardised decisions, which is why it usually takes a decade to build and cannot be carried out of the building. The tell is your own alumni founding competitors that reach parity quickly. The obvious reading — that consistently better operating metrics prove process power — ignores that metrics measure the output, while the barrier question is entirely about the reproducibility of the input.

10. The moat's most useful output is a list of customers you should lose

Once the premium is decomposed by segment, some segments will show a defended premium below zero — meaning you cannot profitably hold them against an informed alternative at any price you would be willing to charge. The expert move is deliberate de-selection: concede those accounts early, cleanly and cheaply, rather than funding their defence out of the margin earned on protected ones. The tell of the amateur is uniform pricing across segments whose switching costs differ by an order of magnitude. The obvious reading — that losing customers is always a failure — misreads the arithmetic: defending an undefendable segment is a transfer from your protected customers to your competitor's, executed at your own expense.

7. What actually differs by product type and company stage

Begin with what does not differ, because most treatments of this topic overstate the variation. The arithmetic of the indifference price is identical everywhere: in every business, the defensible premium equals the buyer's cost of switching, amortised over the horizon the buyer actually uses, plus the value of any performance difference the buyer can perceive and monetise, plus the cost disadvantage a rival cannot avoid. What changes is who holds the pen and which term dominates.

In consumer products the dominant term is perceptual and the horizon is short, so branding and network economies do most of the work; the distinguishing feature is that switching costs are measured in seconds and habits rather than rupees, which makes them simultaneously small per occasion and enormous in aggregate. In B2B and enterprise, the dominant term is integration and audit: workflows, data history, compliance evidence and personnel training, all of which are genuinely costly to unwind, and all of which can be neutralised by a buyer large enough to fund the unwinding — enterprise moats are strong against the middle of the market and weak against its top. In platforms and marketplaces, the dominant term is liquidity, subject to the locality and threshold effects above, and the characteristic failure is multi-homing: the moat lives not in the count of participants but in whatever makes a participant's second listing not worth the effort. In hardware and physical goods, the dominant terms are supply-chain position, tooling amortisation and aftermarket structure, and the characteristic tension is that the aftermarket lock which creates the moat is the same structure that attracts regulatory attention and customer resentment. In AI products, the capability layer commoditises fastest, so the durable terms are data rights, workflow embedding, distribution and permission — and the honest statement is that the field does not yet have enough completed competitive cycles to know which of these persists.

Stage changes the available set rather than the arithmetic. A three-year-old company has no scale, no accumulated switching costs, no brand history and no process depth; its only genuine options are counter-positioning — a model the incumbent cannot copy without hurting itself — or a cornered resource it can lock up cheaply because nobody larger considers it worth locking. Bhupendra at this stage has neither, which is the real finding of its analysis. A mature company like Bhavika has the opposite pathology: several powers on the slide, of which one has quietly saturated, one expires on a date nobody has diarised, and one is being given away through discount authority. The stage-specific discipline for the young firm is to acquire a barrier before it needs one; for the mature firm, to audit the barriers it believes it already has.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

a. Bhavika's cornered resource: buying time at a known price

The membrane exclusivity was worth ₹9 per test across 26.0 million tests, or ₹23.4 crore of gross profit a year, and it expired in March 2029 — thirty months out. The supplier offered an extension to 2034 for a ₹34 crore prepayment. The naive calculation is favourable: ₹34 crore buys five additional years of a ₹23.4 crore annual benefit. The expert calculation is less comfortable. The benefit is not ₹23.4 crore a year for five years; it is the difference between the world with exclusivity and the world without, and in the world without, Bhavika's second-source qualification (2.3× membrane cost, 6.1% CV) would still let it hold perhaps ₹4 of the ₹9. So the true incremental benefit is ₹5 per test — ₹13.0 crore a year, decaying as compatibles improve — which against ₹34 crore paid today yields a payback near three years and an internal rate in the high teens: worth doing, but not the obvious layup the ₹23.4 crore figure suggested. The second-order effect is the one that decided it: signing a seven-year exclusive tells the supplier precisely how much the contract is worth to Bhavika, and guarantees a harder negotiation in 2034. The team's resolution was to sign a shorter four-year extension at ₹19 crore and simultaneously fund second-source qualification, deliberately paying more per year for the option of needing the supplier less.

b. Bhupendra's density play: buying a threshold rather than a customer

Of the two proposals on Kavita's table, only one could be evaluated as a barrier purchase. Concentrating ₹78 crore of subsidy across six corridors — rather than spreading it over fourteen cities — would move all six from a mean of 210 trucks per week to a modelled 640, clearing the broker-parity threshold with margin. The modelled effects: match time from 8.4 to 4.1 hours, fill rate from 63% to 81%, empty-return from 29% to 19%. The commercial consequence is that a fleet owner's realised earnings per truck per month rise by roughly ₹18,400, which is what allows Bhupendra to sustain a 3.6% take rate on those lanes rather than 3.1%. Corridor booking value on the six lanes was ₹610 crore and modelled to reach ₹1,180 crore within eight quarters at that service level. Contribution moves from ₹18.9 crore to ₹42.5 crore a year — an incremental ₹23.6 crore against ₹78 crore spent, a payback near 3.3 years, and, crucially, a barrier that a rival must now overcome on those specific lanes rather than in general. Spread across fourteen cities, the identical ₹78 crore lifts nothing above threshold and buys usage that disappears when the subsidy stops. Same money, same market, entirely different asset.

c. Bhoomik Storefronts: a benefit bought without a barrier

Bhoomik Storefronts, founded in Jaipur in 2019, sold hosted online storefronts, payments and logistics integration to direct-to-consumer brands. Between 2021 and 2023 it spent ₹120 crore on brand marketing on the explicit thesis that it was building two powers at once: brand, and a network effect through its merchant app ecosystem. Both claims failed the tests in section 4. The app "ecosystem" contained 31 applications, of which four accounted for 88% of installs, and all four were available on competing platforms within a year — there was no cross-side effect, because merchants did not choose Bhoomik to reach app developers, and developers did not build for Bhoomik because of merchant count; they built because a channel partner paid them to. The brand spend produced excellent awareness and no pricing power: 68% of merchants ran a second storefront in parallel, and Bhoomik's win/loss data showed price as the decisive factor in 71% of losses. The numbers deteriorated in the pattern the theory predicts. Monthly logo churn reached 4.1%. Net revenue retention fell to 89%. Customer acquisition cost was ₹1.9 lakh against a 31-month payback — which is to say the company was buying customers it could not hold for long enough to pay for them, a condition that is arithmetically unsurvivable.

The recovery is more instructive than the failure. In 2024 the founders stopped brand spend entirely, cut headcount by 19% and accepted a 22% revenue decline in the transition year — and then asked the decomposition question properly: across their whole customer base, was there any place where a barrier already existed that they had not been charging for? There was. The cohort of merchants who had adopted Bhoomik's settlement-reconciliation module — matching payment-gateway settlements, courier remittances, marketplace payouts and GST e-invoicing records into a single auditable ledger — churned at 0.9% a month against 4.1% for everyone else, because unwinding eighteen months of reconciled financial history before a statutory audit is a genuine, dateable, expensive event. The company rebuilt its pricing and its roadmap around that module, made it the default rather than an add-on, and deliberately conceded the storefront-only segment. By late 2025 churn was 1.6% a month blended, net revenue retention 118%, and payback 14 months. The lesson is not that brand is a weak power. It is that Bhoomik had bought benefit with no barrier for three years and ₹120 crore, and the recovery consisted of finding the one place a barrier already existed and moving the price to it.
