10. Where experts genuinely disagree

These are not resolved, and a practitioner who presents them as resolved is signalling that they have read one book.

Are there seven powers, or effectively two? The Greenwald position, steelmanned, is that customer captivity and economies of scale (and a residual supply-side cost advantage) exhaust the real barriers, and that Helmer's other categories are labels for these: branding is captivity through habit, switching costs are captivity through cost, process power is a cost advantage, network economies are scale on the demand side. The evidence is that when you examine long-lived franchises, the durable ones almost always have local scale plus captive customers, and firms that claim the exotic powers without those two usually decay. The Helmer position, steelmanned, is that the categories differ in how you obtain them and therefore in what a management team should do, which is the entire point of a practitioner framework — counter-positioning and cornered resource in particular describe acquisition paths that "captivity plus scale" cannot generate as advice. What would settle it: a systematic study showing that firms categorised as holding one of the five "extra" powers, but lacking local scale and captivity, sustain excess returns at rates indistinguishable from firms with neither. Nobody has produced that study.

Is durable advantage getting shorter? The transient-advantage camp points to compressing product cycles, falling capital requirements for software, and evidence of shortening persistence in technology-exposed industries; its practical recommendation is to build a portfolio of temporary advantages and to institutionalise disengagement. The opposing camp points to the widening dispersion of economic profit across firms — the top decile capturing an ever-greater share, with unusual persistence at the top — and argues that advantage has become more durable for a smaller number of firms, not less durable in general. These two claims are not straightforwardly contradictory (the mean can fall while the top tail fattens), but practitioners reach opposite conclusions from them about how long a moat-driven investment horizon should be, and the disagreement is genuine.

Do network effects still produce winner-take-all outcomes? The sceptical case is strong: multi-homing is cheap, data portability is increasingly mandated, APIs let a challenger bootstrap on an incumbent's own network, and several categories once assumed to tip have settled into stable oligopoly. The defence is that the relevant effect was never raw user count but default distribution and the habit of first resort, which have if anything strengthened. Kavita's data supports the sceptics on her supply side and the defenders on her demand side, within one company — which is itself the useful observation.

Does AI raise or lower barriers? One camp holds that it lowers them decisively: capability that took a decade to build can be approximated in months, so every advantage grounded in accumulated technical skill is being marked down, and what remains is distribution and proprietary data rights. The other holds that it raises them to historic highs, because frontier capability now requires capital, compute and data-licensing access available to very few, producing barriers more absolute than anything the software era knew. For this to be settled we would need to see whether the workflow and data advantages built on top of models prove durable once the underlying models converge — evidence that will take several more competitive cycles to accumulate. Anyone claiming certainty here in 2026 is extrapolating.

Is brand a power or a rent on past performance? The sceptic argues that measured brand premiums usually collapse under controlled comparison, and that what looks like brand is really accumulated switching costs, distribution advantage or genuine quality difference misattributed. The defender points to categories where blind and branded preferences diverge persistently and where a premium survives full information for decades. Both can produce examples; neither has a general test that the other accepts.

11. What mastery looks like in practice

Someone who has merely studied this topic can name the seven powers and classify a company correctly. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in six observable ways. They quote a number instead of a category, and the number has a denominator. They state the arena as a cell — segment, occasion, substitute — before making any claim, and they notice when a colleague's claim has silently changed arenas mid-argument. They carry a renewal calendar and treat every contractual barrier as a dated liability rather than an asset. They read price realisation by segment before they read satisfaction scores, because the first is a measurement of the moat and the second is a measurement of the mood. They decide which customers to lose, explicitly and early, and can defend that decision with the segment-level defended premium. And they war-game from the copier's profit-and-loss statement rather than their own — asking what it would cost a specific, named rival to neutralise a specific mechanism, and whether that rival's board would approve the spend — because a barrier is a statement about someone else's economics, and any analysis that never leaves your own financial model has not tested it.

There is a seventh habit that is harder to see and more diagnostic than the rest: they write down, in advance, what would prove them wrong. Meera's version, drafted before the board paper, was one line — "if a distributor begins funding NABL revalidation for switching labs, our switching-cost component is zero and we should assume it within two quarters". That sentence is worth more than any amount of confidence about the strength of the franchise, because it converts a belief into something the operating review can detect.

12. What each of them decided

Meera rejected the authentication chip. Her reasoning was not primarily legal, though her counsel's note mattered: the chip could not be retrofitted to the 4,820 analysers already in the field, which meant it addressed none of the ₹48 crore of gross profit actually under attack, and it would land as coercion with precisely the chain-procurement buyers whose dual-sourcing mandates made them the least protected and the most vocal segment. She proposed instead a four-part plan that follows directly from the decomposition. First, segment the price rather than cutting it: hold ₹78 on the BH-5 platform, where patent life, membrane exclusivity and process advantage together defend ₹25 of a ₹34 gap, and reprice the BH-3 cartridge to ₹57 — conceding the ₹9 undefended and ₹12 more, deliberately, while remaining ₹13 above the compatible on the strength of the quality difference. Second, make that quality difference contractual and legible: a certified third-party programme with published precision standards and an EQAS-linked warranty, which converts a technical fact into a purchasing criterion a lab manager can put in a file. Third, extend the membrane exclusivity by four years at ₹19 crore while funding a second source, buying the option of needing the supplier less. Fourth, move the barrier forward rather than defending the old one: a connected quality-control subscription that accumulates each lab's precision history in a form auditors accept, which raises switching costs where they are cheapest to raise and does so on the platform that still has patent life to protect it. The plan conceded roughly ₹21 crore of BH-3 revenue over two years. It protected, on Meera's own arithmetic, about ₹19 crore of annual gross profit that the chip strategy would have lost anyway, more slowly and with worse company.

Kavita's decision was less complete, and she said so to her board. She allocated the ₹78 crore to the six corridors rather than fourteen cities, on the argument that only threshold-clearing density creates an asset a rival must overcome rather than usage a rival can rent. She declined the fuel-card credit product in its proposed form, because the barrier belonged to the NBFC partner and would be available to her competitors within two quarters of proving itself. But she recorded a dissent from her own decision in the minutes: the credit product was the only proposal on the table that would convert a local, thresholded, multi-homed network effect into a per-fleet-owner switching cost, and if Bhupendra could ever own the underwriting rather than rent it, the calculation would reverse. She asked for the analysis to be brought back in March with the lending economics modelled on the assumption that Bhupendra held the book itself. Whether that is patience or procrastination is exactly the sort of judgement this framework helps you state precisely and cannot make for you.

Discussion questions

  • Meera's decomposition gives her a defended ceiling of ₹69 against a current price of ₹78. Is deliberately conceding the undefended ₹9 an act of discipline or an unforced surrender of margin that a more aggressive commercial strategy could have held for another three years? What evidence would distinguish the two, and when would it arrive?
  • Bhupendra's network effect is local, thresholded and undermined by 71% supply-side multi-homing. Under what conditions is a marketplace with those properties a better business than a straightforward brokerage that owns its supply — and is Kavita's corridor concentration a step toward a moat, or an expensive way of postponing the discovery that she does not have one?
  • Bhoomik's recovery consisted of finding a barrier that already existed and repricing around it, at the cost of a 22% revenue decline. Suppose the reconciliation cohort had not existed. What, if anything, should the founders have done differently in 2021 — and does your answer imply that the ₹120 crore of brand spend was a mistake, or a reasonable bet that failed?
